newsitem.title: GREECE: Greece welcomes U.S. warning to Turkey.
newsitem.headline: Greece welcomes U.S. warning to Turkey.

text.p: Greece on Friday welcomed a U.S. warning to Turkey to stop threatening the independent island of Cyprus.
Athens also brushed off new Turkish threats to strike at a planned Russian anti-aircraft missile system on Cyprus if the Nicosia government went ahead with the purchase.
Foreign Ministry officials said Greece was determined to keep its composure in the face of what they described as "a cultivated climate of crisis".

Deputy Foreign Minister George Papandreou told reporters Washington had sent "a clear message to Turkey that it needs to conform with international law and respect other states in the region and Greece's borders".
Senior Foreign Ministry officials said Athens was determined to avoid a war of words by downplaying Turkey's statements and not giving in to a climate of crisis.
"We don't want to answer this continuous repetition of provocative statements. Very little is new in what Turkey is saying," one official told Reuters.

Turkish Foreign Minister Tansu Ciller has said Ankara would strike at the missile systems if they were deployed and Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash threatened to integrate a disputed no-man's-land into the Turkish sector of the island.

Turkey invaded Cyprus in 1974 after a brief Greek Cypriot coup inspired by the military then ruling Athens. Around 30,000 troops are based in north Cyprus, declared a breakaway Turkish Cypriot state in 1983 but recognised only by Ankara.
"These offensive missiles will definitely not be deployed. If they are deployed we will do what is needed, if that means they need to be hit they will be hit," Ciller said.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns issued a stern warning to Turkey over the threat to use force.

"There can be no question that Turkey must respect the rules of the road here, which are no country, and specifically in this case Turkey, should threaten the use of military force against Cyprus; no country, specifically here Turkey, should undertake military force against Cyprus," he told reporters.

He had earlier criticised Cyprus for the purchase of the S-300 missile systems, which could neutralise Turkish air superiority over the militarily divided island, saying it did not contribute to efforts to reach a peaceful solution.

Greece and Cyprus have brushed off the criticism, saying it was a double standard to worry about a purely defensive system in the south while allowing 30,000 heavily armed Turkish troops in the north.

Washington, concerned about the renewed tension between NATO members Greece and Turkey, said it would send Carey Cavanaugh, who heads the State Department's office of southern European affairs, to Cyprus on Sunday and Monday.
Cavanaugh is also expected to visit Athens.
